questions.stem: The nephron:

options.label: B
options.text: is lined by a single layer of epithelial cells

options.label: D
options.text: absorbs more ions and molecules than it secretes

questions.why: Nephron tubules have a single epithelial layer that reabsorbs most filtered water and solute while secreting selected substances. Hormones regulate tubular transport, and nephron-associated structures participate in endocrine functions such as renin release and calcitriol production.

notes.A: Juxtaglomerular cells secrete renin, and proximal tubular cells produce calcitriol. These functions are associated with the nephron and its vasculature.
notes.B: The tubular wall is largely a single epithelial cell layer whose cell type varies according to the function of each segment.
notes.C: Hormones can regulate transport along the nephron. Aldosterone, for example, increases sodium reabsorption in the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron.
notes.D: Most filtered water, sodium and small nutrients are reabsorbed. The tubules also secrete selected substances such as hydrogen ions and organic anions.

questions.stem: The control of water excretion in the kidney is controlled by:
questions.why: Antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin, directly controls variable water reabsorption in the collecting ducts. It activates V2 receptors on principal cells, increasing apical aquaporin-2 and decreasing the amount of water excreted.

notes.B: Osmotic control of vasopressin is centred in hypothalamic pathways. The medulla oblongata does not directly set collecting-duct water permeability.
notes.C: Plasma osmolality and effective volume influence vasopressin release. The hormone provides the direct signal to the collecting duct.
notes.D: Plasma sodium contributes to tonicity and can influence vasopressin release. It does not directly insert aquaporin-2.
notes.E: Potassium balance affects renal ion handling and can modify concentrating ability in disease. It is not the principal direct control of water excretion.

questions.stem: The kidneys have a direct effect on which of the following?

options.label: B
options.text: how much water a person excretes

questions.why: The kidneys regulate water and sodium excretion, which affects circulating volume and blood pressure. They also release renin and regulate acid–base balance by reclaiming bicarbonate and excreting net acid.

notes.A: Renal sodium handling and the renin–angiotensin system influence arterial blood pressure.
notes.B: Changes in tubular water reabsorption determine how much filtered water leaves in the urine.
notes.C: Regulation of sodium and water content helps determine extracellular fluid and blood volume.
notes.D: The kidneys contribute to blood pH by reclaiming bicarbonate and excreting acid as ammonium and titratable acid.

questions.stem: Urinary volume is increased with:
questions.why: Acute alcohol intake can suppress vasopressin release, and posterior pituitary injury can reduce its delivery to blood. Both can increase water excretion. Hyperglycaemia past the renal reabsorptive capacity causes glucosuria and osmotic diuresis.

notes.A: Acute alcohol intake can decrease vasopressin release and temporarily reduce collecting-duct water reabsorption.
notes.B: When filtered glucose exceeds reabsorptive capacity, glucose remains in the lumen and increases water loss by osmotic diuresis.
notes.C: Aldosterone promotes distal sodium reabsorption. Increased aldosterone is not a general cause of increased urine volume.
notes.D: Posterior pituitary or stalk injury can impair vasopressin release, increasing excretion of dilute urine.

questions.stem: The antidiuretic hormone (ADH):

options.label: C
options.text: increases the reabsorption of water in the proximal tubules

options.label: D
options.text: is synthesized in the posterior pituitary gland

questions.why: Vasopressin increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2, allowing more water to be reabsorbed into the hypertonic medulla. It normally decreases urine volume and allows the urine to become more concentrated.

notes.A: Water removal from tubular fluid generally increases urine osmolality when an adequate medullary gradient is present.
notes.C: Proximal water reabsorption largely follows solute and is not the principal adjustable site for vasopressin.
notes.D: Vasopressin is synthesised in hypothalamic neurons. It is transported to the posterior pituitary for storage and release.
notes.E: Vasopressin mainly regulates water balance. Urinary glucose rises when the filtered load exceeds proximal glucose transport or when that transport is impaired.

questions.stem: Regarding the kidneys:

options.label: A
options.text: there are 1.3 million nephrons in each kidney

options.label: C
options.text: they receive 12% of the cardiac output at rest

options.label: D
options.text: more blood flows through the renal cortex than the renal medulla

questions.why: Each kidney has ~1 million nephrons. The cortex receives the vast majority of renal blood flow (~90%).

notes.A: True (about 1 million), but D is also true.
notes.B: Aldosterone is adrenal.
notes.C: They receive about 20–25%.
notes.D: True, but A is also true.

questions.stem: The glomerular capillaries have the following functions:
questions.why: Glomerular capillaries form a filtrate when hydrostatic pressure drives water and small solutes across the filtration barrier into Bowman’s space. This primary urine is modified later by tubular reabsorption and secretion.

notes.A: Water and small solutes are filtered from plasma. The glomerular capillary barrier retains blood cells and most large proteins.
notes.B: Hormones such as renin come from specialised renal cells. The chief function of the glomerular capillary tuft is filtration.
notes.C: Water moves across the glomerular barrier by bulk filtration. Tubular secretion refers to a separate transfer into the nephron lumen.
notes.D: Primary urine is the initial glomerular filtrate entering Bowman’s space before tubular processing.

questions.stem: The obligatory urine volume (the minimum needed to excrete the daily solute load) is about:
questions.why: Obligatory urine volume depends on how much solute must be excreted and how concentrated the kidney can make the urine. A daily load of about 600 milliosmoles divided by a maximal urine osmolality near 1,200 milliosmoles per kilogram gives roughly 0.5 litres.

notes.A: In 100 millilitres, a typical daily solute load would require a concentration far above normal human concentrating capacity.
notes.B: At a maximal osmolality near 1,200 milliosmoles per kilogram, 300 millilitres cannot carry a typical 600-milliosmole load.
notes.C: About 1.5 litres is a common daily output with ordinary fluid intake. The theoretical minimum for a typical load is lower.
notes.D: A person can produce 2.5 litres with higher intake, but this exceeds the minimum volume needed for typical solute excretion.

questions.stem: Blood flow per gram of tissue at rest is highest in the:
questions.why: The kidneys receive roughly one fifth of resting cardiac output despite accounting for a small fraction of body mass. This high perfusion per gram provides plasma for filtration and exceeds that of the other listed organs under usual resting conditions.

notes.A: The brain has a high total blood flow and sustained oxygen demand, but its blood flow per gram is below the renal value at rest.
notes.B: The liver receives high total flow through the portal vein and hepatic artery. Because of its larger mass, its usual flow per gram is lower.
notes.D: The heart has high oxygen extraction and can increase coronary flow with effort. Resting flow per gram is lower than for the kidneys.
notes.E: Resting skin perfusion varies strongly with temperature and is usually much lower per gram than renal perfusion.

questions.stem: Renal blood flow depends on:
questions.why: Renal blood flow is directly dependent on systemic arterial pressure (though autoregulated within a range).

notes.A: Part of control, not the determinant.
notes.B: Acts through tubuloglomerular feedback.
notes.C: Dilatation RAISES flow, but pressure is the driver.
notes.E: This raises resistance and LOWERS flow.

questions.stem: Kidneys produce:
questions.why: The kidneys produce erythropoietin in response to hypoxia to stimulate RBC production.

notes.B: ADH comes from the hypothalamus.
notes.C: Most conversion happens in the lungs.
notes.D: ANP comes from the heart.
notes.E: The kidney makes CALCITRIOL; cholecalciferol is made in the skin.

questions.stem: The kidneys filter from the blood every day about:
questions.why: A representative glomerular filtration rate in a healthy adult is about 125 millilitres per minute. Over 1,440 minutes this is about 180 litres of filtrate per day. Most is reabsorbed, so final urine output is much smaller.

notes.A: One litre per day is closer to final urine output than to the volume of plasma water filtered before reabsorption.
notes.C: Eighteen litres per day corresponds to a filtration rate of about 12.5 millilitres per minute, far below the standard teaching estimate.
notes.D: Fifty litres a day corresponds to roughly 35 millilitres per minute. This is well below the representative healthy adult value.
notes.E: Eight litres per day represents a very low filtration rate rather than the usual healthy adult daily filtrate volume.

questions.stem: Direct control of water excretion in the kidneys is controlled by:
questions.why: Vasopressin directly adjusts urine water excretion by activating V2 receptors and increasing aquaporin-2 in collecting-duct principal cells. More water is then reabsorbed, provided a medullary osmotic gradient is present.

notes.B: Hypothalamic neurons synthesise vasopressin. The medulla oblongata does not provide the direct collecting-duct signal.
notes.C: Aldosterone increases distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Vasopressin directly controls variable water permeability.
notes.D: A rise in plasma sodium often raises tonicity and promotes vasopressin release. This is an upstream stimulus.
notes.E: The adrenal cortex produces aldosterone and other steroids. The direct adjustable water-permeability signal comes from vasopressin.

questions.stem: Long-standing obstruction of the urethra may cause:

options.label: C
options.text: dilation of the ureters and reduction of the glomerular filtration rate

options.label: D
options.text: increase and reduction of the glomerular filtration rate

options.label: E
options.text: a decrease in residual volume in the bladder

questions.why: Urinary obstruction increases pressure backwards, causing hydroureter (dilation) and eventually damaging the kidneys, reducing GFR.

notes.A: Prostate enlargement is a CAUSE.
notes.B: The bladder muscle HYPERtrophies.
notes.D: Contradictory.
notes.E: Residual volume RISES.

questions.stem: Emptying of the bladder may be less effective if:

options.label: A
options.text: the sympathetic nerves carrying afferent information from bladder to the spinal cord are cut

options.label: B
options.text: the pelvic nerves are cut or anticholinergic drugs are administered

options.label: D
options.text: alpha- adrenergic receptor antagonists are administered

options.label: E
options.text: beta- adrenergic receptor blockers are administered

questions.why: Parasympathetic fibres in the pelvic nerves contract the detrusor chiefly via muscarinic receptors. Cutting those nerves or giving antimuscarinic drugs weakens detrusor activation and can make bladder emptying less effective.

notes.A: Bladder fullness reaches the sacral cord chiefly through afferents in pelvic nerves. The main detrusor motor pathway is pelvic parasympathetic.
notes.C: Muscarinic agonism can promote detrusor contraction. Blocking these receptors is the more direct way to impair contraction.
notes.D: Alpha-adrenergic blockade can decrease bladder outlet resistance and facilitate flow in some forms of obstruction.
notes.E: Beta-3 receptor activation helps relax the detrusor during filling. Beta blockade is not the standard mechanism for loss of the voiding contraction.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic renal failure usually has:

options.label: A
options.text: an increased blood urea and blood uric acid

options.label: D
options.text: an increased acid- base disturbance when he or she vomits

options.label: E
options.text: an increased acid- base problem on a low protein diet

questions.why: Chronic kidney failure decreases filtration and excretion of nitrogenous waste. Serum urea usually rises, and uric acid often rises because renal urate clearance falls. Diet, medications and other factors can modify the measured values.

notes.B: Reduced renal urate clearance often increases rather than decreases serum uric acid.
notes.C: Creatinine clearance generally falls as renal filtration is lost, even though tubular secretion can affect the estimate.
notes.D: Vomiting removes gastric acid and can cause alkalosis. It does not predictably worsen the underlying acid–base disorder of kidney failure.
notes.E: Lower dietary protein may reduce dietary acid and nitrogen loads. It is not a usual cause of a worsening renal acid–base disturbance.

questions.stem: Cutting the sympathetic nerves to the bladder may cause:

options.label: B
options.text: loss of tone in the internal sphincter of the bladder and loss of pain sensation in the bladder

options.label: C
options.text: loss of tone in the external sphincter of the bladder

options.label: D
options.text: increased pain sensation in the bladder

questions.why: Sympathetic nerves control the internal sphincter (contraction) and carry pain afferents. Cutting them causes the sphincter to lose tone.

notes.A: Emptying is parasympathetic.
notes.C: The external sphincter is somatic (pudendal).
notes.D: Pain is LOST.
notes.E: Not a recognised effect.

questions.stem: Acute renal failure differs from chronic renal failure in that:

options.label: A
options.text: potassium retention tends to be more severe

options.label: B
options.text: blood urea levels tend to be higher

options.label: C
options.text: depression of bone marrow activity is unlikely to occur

options.label: D
options.text: metabolic acidosis is usually not a problem

questions.why: Acute renal failure often causes severe, rapid hyperkalemia, which can be life-threatening.

notes.B: Urea rises more in chronic failure.
notes.C: Marrow depression (no EPO) can occur.
notes.D: Acidosis IS a problem.
notes.E: Protein restriction helps.

questions.stem: The inhibition of the antidiuretic hormone (ADH), say by alcohol, would have what affect?

options.label: E
options.text: reduction in water reabsorption by the kidneys

questions.why: Reducing vasopressin decreases aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct principal cells. The ducts then reabsorb less water, increasing the volume of relatively dilute urine. Acute alcohol intake can produce this effect.

notes.A: Afferent arteriolar constriction lowers perfusion of the glomerulus. It is not the direct response of collecting-duct cells to reduced vasopressin.
notes.B: Lower vasopressin typically increases water diuresis by reducing collecting-duct permeability.
notes.C: Vasopressin promotes water conservation when elevated. Suppressing it has the opposite effect.
notes.D: Efferent arteriolar tone affects filtration and is controlled by factors such as angiotensin II. This is not the primary antidiuretic mechanism.

questions.stem: The formation of the final urine is achieved by:
questions.why: Urine formation begins with glomerular filtration. Tubular reabsorption returns selected substances to blood, and tubular secretion moves additional substances into tubular fluid. The amount excreted reflects filtration minus reabsorption plus secretion.

notes.A: Diffusion can contribute to tubular transport, but listing it separately omits reabsorption as a major process.
notes.B: Osmosis and diffusion describe transport mechanisms. This list omits glomerular filtration and net tubular secretion.
notes.D: Paracrine signals help regulate renal function. They are not a substitute for tubular reabsorption in the steps of urine formation.
notes.E: Each of the other lists is incomplete. Some include transport mechanisms or regulatory signals in place of a major net process.

questions.stem: Normal diuresis per 24h is about:
questions.why: An adult with ordinary intake commonly produces around 1.5 litres of urine in 24 hours, and about 1.5–2 litres is a reasonable teaching estimate. Output varies with intake, solute excretion and water losses outside the kidney.

notes.A: Five hundred millilitres is closer to an obligatory low volume under typical solute loading than to average daily urine output.
notes.C: Five litres a day is substantially above the usual adult range and can occur with polyuria or high fluid intake.
notes.D: A daily volume near 120–180 litres describes glomerular filtrate before most tubular water is reabsorbed.
notes.E: Fifteen litres per day is far above typical urine output and indicates extreme water or solute diuresis.

questions.stem: Volume of plasma, totally cleared from a substance when passing through the kidneys per unit time is called:
questions.why: Renal clearance is the virtual volume of plasma from which the kidneys remove a substance per unit time. It equals urine concentration multiplied by urine flow, divided by plasma concentration.

notes.A: Diuresis refers to urine production or increased urine flow. It does not specify removal of a particular substance from plasma.
notes.B: Final urine formation describes the combined nephron processes. Clearance quantifies the net removal of a specific solute.
notes.C: Glomerular filtration rate is the volume of filtrate formed per time. It equals clearance only for an appropriate marker handled by filtration alone.
notes.D: Transport maximum is a rate of saturable tubular transport, generally expressed as amount per time rather than plasma volume per time.

questions.stem: All the following substances are synthesized in the kidneys, except:
questions.why: Antidiuretic hormone is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. The kidney responds to it at V2 receptors. The other options describe substances produced or generated within renal tissue.

notes.A: Renal cyclooxygenase pathways generate prostaglandins that help regulate vascular and tubular function.
notes.B: The renal kallikrein–kinin system generates local kinins by cleaving kininogen. This is local production by processing a precursor.
notes.D: Proximal tubular cells use 1-alpha-hydroxylase to form calcitriol from 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
notes.E: Juxtaglomerular granular cells produce renin and release it when renal perfusion or other signals indicate a need to activate the system.

questions.stem: The secretion of less than 500 ml final urine per 24 hours is termed:
questions.why: Oliguria means abnormally low final urine output. A daily volume below roughly 400–500 millilitres is a common adult definition. Clinical criteria also use output relative to body weight and the duration of low flow.

notes.A: Polyuria is an abnormally large urine volume, commonly more than about three litres a day in adults.
notes.B: Polydipsia means excessive thirst or fluid intake and is distinct from measured urine output.
notes.D: Anuria describes almost no urine output. Its threshold is far lower than the range generally termed oliguria.
notes.E: Glucosuria is the presence of glucose in urine. It does not describe a low urine volume.

questions.stem: The nerve center, controlling the secretion of urine is located in:

options.label: C
options.text: the thoracic segments of the spinal cord

options.label: D
options.text: the sacral segments of the spinal cord

options.label: E
options.text: the lumbar segments of the spinal cord

questions.why: Micturition (urination) reflexes are integrated in the sacral segments of the spinal cord (S2-S4).

notes.A: The pontine centre modulates, but the reflex is sacral.
notes.B: Not the micturition centre.
notes.C: Thoracolumbar outflow is sympathetic (storage).
notes.E: Lumbar outflow is sympathetic.

questions.stem: The glomerulus:

options.label: A
options.text: has both afferent and efferent arterioles

options.label: B
options.text: contains capillaries, which are at a higher hydrostatic pressure than the peritubular capillaries

options.label: C
options.text: filters 20% of the renal plasma flow

questions.why: All statements are true. The glomerulus is a high-pressure capillary bed between two arterioles, filtering about 20% of renal plasma flow.

notes.A: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.B: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.C: True, but so are the other statements.
notes.D: True, but so are the other statements.

questions.stem: Stimulation of the sympathetic nerves cause the following effects:
questions.why: Strong renal sympathetic stimulation constricts renal arterioles, especially the afferent arteriole. This can lower glomerular capillary pressure and filtration. Sympathetic promotion of tubular sodium reabsorption can also contribute to lower urine output.

notes.A: Renal sympathetic activation can lower urine output by reducing filtration and favouring sodium and water retention.
notes.B: Strong afferent constriction reduces pressure transmitted to the glomerular capillaries, decreasing the net filtration pressure.
notes.C: Glucosuria primarily reflects filtered glucose exceeding reabsorptive capacity or impaired proximal transport. It is not an obligatory sympathetic response.
notes.D: A decrease in urine glucose is not an expected general effect of renal sympathetic activation. Urine glucose is normally minimal.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances has the highest renal clearance?
questions.why: At a low plasma concentration, para-aminohippurate is filtered and also avidly secreted by proximal tubules. This removes most PAH from plasma that perfuses the functioning kidney, so its clearance approaches effective renal plasma flow and exceeds GFR.

notes.B: Glucose clearance is normally near zero because the proximal tubule reabsorbs almost all filtered glucose below the transport threshold.
notes.C: Some filtered urea is reabsorbed, so urea clearance is generally below glomerular filtration rate and therefore well below PAH clearance.
notes.D: Most filtered water is reabsorbed along the nephron. Urine flow is much lower than the effective renal plasma flow.
notes.E: Inulin is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Its clearance measures GFR, which is only part of the effective renal plasma flow.

questions.stem: Which of the following is involved in the regulation of glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?

options.label: D
options.text: chloride transport at the macula densa

questions.why: GFR depends on glomerular pressure, which responds to afferent and efferent arteriolar resistance. The juxtaglomerular apparatus includes the macula densa, which senses tubular sodium chloride uptake and feeds back on afferent tone and renin release.

notes.A: The juxtaglomerular apparatus links distal tubular sensing with arteriolar responses and renin release.
notes.B: Afferent dilation tends to increase glomerular capillary pressure, whereas afferent constriction decreases it.
notes.C: Moderate efferent constriction can maintain or raise glomerular pressure. Marked constriction may ultimately lower filtration by reducing flow.
notes.D: The macula densa uses NKCC2 to sense luminal sodium chloride. This contributes to feedback regulation of glomerular filtration.

questions.stem: Increase in GFR occurs when there is:
questions.why: Plasma proteins create oncotic pressure in glomerular capillaries, opposing filtration. A fall in their concentration decreases this opposing force and tends to raise GFR when the other determinants stay constant.

notes.A: Strong sympathetic stimulation decreases renal perfusion through vasoconstriction and generally lowers filtration.
notes.B: Reduced renal blood flow can lower filtration or increase the rise of oncotic pressure along the capillary. Decreased flow alone does not explain a rise in GFR.
notes.D: Ureteric obstruction raises pressure upstream in the nephron, which opposes filtration into Bowman’s space.
notes.E: Hypoproteinaemia provides a mechanism for increased filtration by reducing the pressure that draws water back toward the capillary.

questions.stem: The renal clearance of a substance:

options.label: A
options.text: is inversely related to its urinary concentration, U

options.label: B
options.text: is directly related to the rate of urine formation, and is expressed in units of volume per unit time

options.label: C
options.text: is directly related to its plasma concentration, P

options.label: E
options.text: must fall in the presence of metabolic poisons

questions.why: Renal clearance is urine concentration multiplied by urine flow and divided by plasma concentration. It has units of volume per time. At fixed urine and plasma concentrations, higher urine flow gives higher calculated clearance.

notes.A: With urine flow and plasma concentration fixed, clearance increases as the urine concentration rises.
notes.C: With the urinary excretion rate fixed, a higher plasma concentration decreases the calculated clearance.
notes.D: Millimetres of mercury are units of pressure. Renal clearance is normally expressed in millilitres per minute.
notes.E: Metabolic inhibition can reduce active secretion or reabsorption. The direction of clearance change depends on how the substance is handled.

questions.stem: When a patient's mean arterial blood pressure falls by 50%:

options.label: C
options.text: there is a decrease in the circulating aldosterone level

questions.why: A sudden fall of mean arterial pressure to half its usual value commonly takes renal perfusion below the autoregulatory range. The systemic baroreflex then increases sympathetic tone and can cause renal vasoconstriction, while filtration and urine output usually fall.

notes.A: With severe hypotension, low perfusion pressure and sympathetic vasoconstriction usually decrease renal blood flow.
notes.B: Below the autoregulatory range, glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure and GFR tend to decrease.
notes.C: Low renal perfusion usually stimulates renin release. Angiotensin II then promotes rather than suppresses aldosterone secretion.
notes.E: Reduced filtration and enhanced salt and water conservation generally decrease urine output during severe hypotension.

questions.stem: Renal blood flow falls:

options.label: A
options.text: about 10% when arterial pressure increases 10% above normal

options.label: B
options.text: about 5% when metabolic activity in the kidney falls by 5%

options.label: E
options.text: gradually from the inner medulla to the outer cortex per unit weight of tissue

questions.why: Emotional stress triggers sympathetic activation, causing renal vasoconstriction and decreased renal blood flow.

notes.A: Autoregulation keeps flow constant.
notes.B: Flow does not track metabolism.
notes.D: Autoregulation buffers a small bleed.
notes.E: Flow is HIGHEST in the cortex.

questions.stem: The renal clearance of:

options.label: A
options.text: inulin provides an estimate of glomerular filtration rate

options.label: B
options.text: chloride increases after an injection of aldosterone

options.label: C
options.text: PAH falls when the PAH load exceeds the Tm for PAH

options.label: D
options.text: urea is higher than that of inulin

options.label: E
options.text: inulin is dependent of its plasma concentration

questions.why: Inulin clearance is the gold standard for measuring GFR because it is freely filtered and neither secreted nor reabsorbed.

notes.B: Aldosterone DECREASES Cl- clearance.
notes.C: PAH clearance falls above Tm, but this does not estimate GFR.
notes.D: Urea is lower (reabsorbed).
notes.E: Inulin clearance is INDEPENDENT of concentration.

questions.stem: The renal clearance:

options.label: A
options.text: of glucose is above 0, if the plasma concentration of a given substance is below 11 mmol·1-1

options.label: B
options.text: of urea is higher than creatinin's one

options.label: C
options.text: of glucose provides an estimate of renal plasma flow

options.label: D
options.text: of phosphate is decreased by parathormonee

questions.why: Proteins are too large to be filtered by the glomerulus, so their clearance is normally zero.

notes.A: Glucose clearance is zero below threshold.
notes.B: Urea is lower.
notes.C: PAH estimates plasma flow.
notes.D: PTH INCREASES phosphate clearance.

questions.stem: The glomerular filtration is estimated via the clearance of:
questions.why: Inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance measures GFR. Creatinine clearance approximates GFR in routine use, with some overestimation because proximal tubules secrete a small amount.

notes.A: Clearance of para-aminohippurate at low levels approximates effective renal plasma flow because PAH is both filtered and secreted.
notes.B: Most filtered glucose is normally reabsorbed, so its clearance is close to zero under usual plasma concentrations.
notes.C: Urea is variably reabsorbed along the nephron. Its clearance is not a direct measure of filtered volume.
notes.E: Most filtered sodium is reabsorbed, and its excretion is tightly regulated. Sodium clearance does not measure GFR.

questions.stem: If the clearance of a substance is higher than the clearance of inulin:

options.label: A
options.text: the substance is additionally reabsorbed in the tubules

options.label: B
options.text: the substance is additionally secreted in the tubules

options.label: C
options.text: the substance is either additionally reabsorbed or secreted

options.label: D
options.text: the substance is transported with proteins in the tubules

options.label: E
options.text: the substance is secreted in the proximal more than in the distal tubule

questions.why: Inulin clearance represents GFR. For a freely filtered substance handled by filtration and tubular transport, a clearance greater than GFR means excretion exceeds the filtered load, so there is net addition by tubular secretion.

notes.A: Net reabsorption decreases excretion relative to the filtered load and tends to lower clearance below inulin clearance.
notes.C: The higher clearance specifies net secretion under the usual assumptions. Net reabsorption would shift the clearance in the opposite direction.
notes.D: Clearance is a comparison of excretion and plasma concentration. It does not identify protein binding or the molecular transport mechanism.
notes.E: Higher clearance shows net secretion but does not locate its site. Separate segmental data are needed to identify the secreting tubule.

questions.stem: If the clearance of a substance is lower than the clearance of inulin:

options.label: A
options.text: the substance is additionally reabsorbed in the tubules

options.label: B
options.text: the substance is neither reabsorbed, neither secreted

options.label: C
options.text: the substance is additionally secreted in the tubules

options.label: D
options.text: the substance is co-transported with proteins in the tubules

options.label: E
options.text: the substance is secreted in the proximal more than in the distal tubule

questions.why: For a freely filtered substance, a clearance below inulin clearance means that urinary excretion is below the filtered load, consistent with net tubular reabsorption. If filtration is restricted by protein binding or size, low clearance alone does not establish reabsorption.

notes.B: A freely filtered substance with neither reabsorption nor secretion has the same clearance as inulin.
notes.C: Net secretion increases urinary excretion above the filtered load and raises clearance relative to GFR, assuming free filtration.
notes.D: A whole-kidney clearance comparison does not identify the membrane transport mechanism or whether a protein is involved.
notes.E: A clearance value does not identify which nephron segment handles a substance or prove that secretion predominates in one segment.

questions.stem: The factors determining glomerular filtration are:
questions.why: Filtration depends on the glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure driving fluid outward and the opposing plasma oncotic and Bowman’s space hydrostatic pressures. GFR also depends on the filtration coefficient, which reflects capillary surface area and permeability.

notes.A: Capillary pressure and plasma oncotic pressure are important, but the list omits hydrostatic pressure in Bowman’s space.
notes.B: Tubular reabsorption is a process downstream of glomerular filtration. It is not one of the Starling pressure terms.
notes.D: Intraabdominal pressure can affect renal haemodynamics in some conditions. It is not the same as the pressure within Bowman’s space.
notes.E: Filtration and reabsorption are processes of urine formation rather than the pressures that determine net filtration.

questions.stem: What is specific about juxtaglomerular nephrons, it is that:

options.label: A
options.text: the glomeruli are located in the inner part of cortex (near medulla)

options.label: B
options.text: have long loops of Henle, reaching papillies

options.label: C
options.text: their efferent arterioles give rise of vasa recta in medulla

questions.why: Juxtamedullary nephrons have glomeruli in the inner cortex next to the medulla and long loops of Henle reaching the papilla, and their efferent arterioles form the vasa recta. Together these make urine concentration possible.

notes.A: True, but so are B and C.
notes.B: True, but so are A and C.
notes.C: True, but so are A and B.
notes.E: D is correct.

questions.stem: Glomerular filtration rate is DECREASED by:

options.label: A
options.text: a rise in mean arterial pressure above 180 mmHg

options.label: D
options.text: moderate constriction of the efferent arteriole

questions.why: Constriction of the afferent arteriole increases resistance before the glomerular capillaries and lowers their hydrostatic pressure. This decreases the driving force for filtration and therefore tends to lower GFR.

notes.A: Above the autoregulatory range, a rise in pressure can be transmitted to glomerular capillaries. It does not ordinarily decrease filtration acutely.
notes.B: A decrease in plasma proteins lowers the oncotic pressure opposing filtration and tends to increase GFR when other factors are fixed.
notes.D: Moderate efferent constriction raises pressure in the glomerular capillaries and can help maintain or increase GFR.
notes.E: Afferent dilation decreases upstream resistance and tends to increase both glomerular capillary pressure and GFR.

questions.stem: The volume of glomerular filtration is about:
questions.why: A standard teaching estimate of adult GFR is about 125 millilitres per minute, corresponding to 180 litres of glomerular filtrate per day. The exact rate varies with age, body size and kidney function.

notes.B: A flow of roughly 600 millilitres per minute is closer to renal plasma flow. The kidneys filter only a fraction of that plasma.
notes.C: About 1.2 litres per minute is closer to total renal blood flow, which includes blood cells and plasma.
notes.D: Five litres per minute is near the total resting cardiac output of an adult and is far above GFR.
notes.E: About 170 litres can be a daily filtrate volume. It is not a plausible volume filtered in one minute.

questions.stem: Glucose reabsorption occurs in the:
questions.why: Filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. SGLT2 takes up most of it in early segments, and SGLT1 recovers much of the remainder downstream within the proximal tubule.

notes.B: The loop of Henle adjusts salt and water handling and creates the medullary gradient. Glucose is normally already reclaimed before this segment.
notes.C: The distal tubule mainly adjusts ion transport. It does not carry out bulk recovery of filtered glucose.
notes.D: The cortical collecting duct adjusts sodium, potassium and water handling. It is not the main site of sodium–glucose cotransport.
notes.E: The medullary collecting duct responds to vasopressin and participates in concentration of urine. It does not reclaim appreciable filtered glucose.

questions.stem: The following occurs in the proximal tubule of the nephron:
questions.why: In normal conditions, the proximal tubule reabsorbs essentially all filtered glucose and about two thirds of filtered sodium and water. Sodium transport is driven by the basolateral sodium–potassium pump, and water follows the osmotic gradient.

notes.A: SGLT2 and SGLT1 normally recover almost all filtered glucose. Glucosuria occurs if the filtered load exceeds transport capacity or transport is impaired.
notes.B: A large fraction of water is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule, largely following solute across a highly water-permeable epithelium.
notes.C: The basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase maintains an inward sodium gradient, allowing active transepithelial sodium reabsorption.
notes.D: Most filtered bicarbonate is reclaimed in this segment. Apical hydrogen ion secretion helps recover it rather than producing net bicarbonate secretion.

questions.stem: Glucose is reabsorbed:
questions.why: Filtered glucose enters proximal tubular cells through sodium–glucose cotransport. The basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase provides the sodium gradient, making apical uptake secondary active transport. Glucose normally exits the cells by facilitated diffusion.

notes.A: Apical uptake is secondary active because sodium moving downhill provides the energy to transport glucose.
notes.B: The basolateral step is facilitated diffusion. Passive transport alone does not account for the uphill apical uptake step.
notes.C: SGLT2 and SGLT1 are sodium–glucose cotransporters that use sodium entry from the lumen to drive glucose uptake.
notes.D: Hydrogen ion exchange supports acid–base transport in the proximal tubule. Filtered glucose is reclaimed by sodium-linked cotransport.

questions.stem: The ascending limb of the loop of Henle is:

options.label: B
options.text: involved in active transport of K+ into the lumen

options.label: C
options.text: involved in active transport of Cl- out of the lumen

options.label: D
options.text: involved in active transport of Na+ into the lumen

questions.why: The thick ascending limb reabsorbs chloride through the apical sodium–potassium–2 chloride cotransporter NKCC2. The basolateral sodium pump powers this indirectly, and chloride exits the cell basolaterally. The segment is relatively impermeable to water, so tubular fluid becomes dilute.

notes.A: Sodium can cross the epithelium and is reabsorbed with potassium and chloride in the thick ascending limb.
notes.B: Some potassium returns to the tubular lumen through ROMK channels. This recycling is through a channel and is not active pumping of potassium into the lumen.
notes.D: Net sodium transport in the thick ascending limb is out of the lumen, in part via apical NKCC2 uptake.
notes.E: Salt is reabsorbed without accompanying water, making fluid at the end of the thick ascending limb relatively dilute.

questions.stem: Water excretion by the kidney is due to:

options.label: C
options.text: passive secretion in the collecting tubules

questions.why: Water reabsorption and excretion occur via osmosis, driven by osmotic gradients.

notes.B: Water is not pumped.
notes.C: Not a mechanism.
notes.D: Water carries solutes by solvent drag, not the other way round.
notes.E: Aquaporins allow osmosis, not facilitated diffusion.

questions.stem: The clearance (or 'renal regulation') of which one of the following is not regulated by a hormone:
questions.why: Sulfate clearance is not directly regulated by a specific hormone in the way Na (aldosterone), K (aldosterone), Ca (PTH), or phosphate (PTH) are.

notes.A: Aldosterone and ANP regulate it.
notes.B: Aldosterone regulates it.
notes.C: PTH regulates it.
notes.D: PTH regulates it.

questions.stem: The countercurrent exchange system includes:

options.label: B
options.text: proximal convoluted tubule and distal convoluted tubule

options.label: C
options.text: loop of Henle and collecting tubule

questions.why: The countercurrent system involves the loop of Henle (multiplier) and the vasa recta (exchanger) to create a concentrated medullary interstitium.

notes.A: These are not countercurrent.
notes.B: These are not countercurrent.
notes.D: These are vessels around the glomerulus.
notes.E: These are outflow.

questions.stem: Tubular reabsorption of a filtered substance is likely to be active rather than passive if:

options.label: A
options.text: its concentration in the tubular fluid is lower than in peritubular capillary blood

options.label: B
options.text: is carried out by the mechanism of simple diffusion

options.label: C
options.text: renal clearance is lower than that of inulin

options.label: D
options.text: renal clearance rises at low plasma levels

options.label: E
options.text: osmolality there is higher than the plasma one

questions.why: If reabsorption moves a solute from a lower luminal concentration to a higher blood concentration, the uphill chemical gradient suggests an energy-dependent step. The electrical gradient or coupling to another solute can also influence the transport mechanism.

notes.B: Simple diffusion is passive and moves a substance down its electrochemical gradient without a direct energy input.
notes.C: A clearance below inulin suggests net reabsorption of a freely filtered solute. It does not identify whether transport is active or passive.
notes.D: Clearance can vary with plasma concentration for multiple reasons, including saturation. That pattern alone does not establish an active mechanism.
notes.E: Total osmolality describes the collective concentration of dissolved particles. It does not identify the driving force for the particular solute.

questions.stem: In the fluid in the distal part of the proximal convoluted tubule:

options.label: A
options.text: urea concentration is higher than in Bowman's capsule

options.label: B
options.text: pH is less than 6 when the kidneys are excreting an acid urine

options.label: C
options.text: glucose concentration is similar to that in plasma

options.label: D
options.text: osmolality is about 25 per cent that of glomerular filtrate

options.label: E
options.text: bicarbonate concentration is higher than in plasma

questions.why: In the proximal tubule, water is reabsorbed more rapidly than urea, even though some urea is also reabsorbed. Removing a larger fraction of water raises the concentration of urea in the fluid remaining relative to the original glomerular filtrate.

notes.B: Proximal bicarbonate reabsorption lowers tubular pH, but the ability to produce very acid urine depends principally on the distal nephron.
notes.C: Glucose is reabsorbed avidly in the proximal tubule. In normal conditions its filtered concentration falls markedly along this segment.
notes.D: Proximal water reabsorption largely follows solute. The tubular fluid is approximately iso-osmotic with plasma.
notes.E: The proximal tubule reclaims most filtered bicarbonate. The remaining luminal bicarbonate concentration is generally lower than at filtration.

questions.stem: Renal tubules normally reabsorb:

options.label: A
options.text: fluids with osmolality lower than the plasma one

options.label: B
options.text: all filtered HCO3- in respiratory alcalosis

questions.why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs almost all filtered proteins (which normally do not pass the glomerular filter in large amounts anyway).

notes.A: Proximal reabsorption is iso-osmotic.
notes.B: In alkalosis HCO3- is EXCRETED.
notes.C: Vague.
notes.E: Far more Cl- than K+ is reabsorbed.

questions.stem: In the nephron, the osmolality of the fluid in the:

options.label: A
options.text: tip of the loop of Henle is less than that of plasma

options.label: B
options.text: Bowman's capsules is less than that in the distal tubules

options.label: C
options.text: collecting duct rises when vasopressin is being secreted

options.label: D
options.text: proximal convoluted tubule rises along its length

options.label: E
options.text: proximal tubule is with lower osmolality than plasma one

questions.why: Vasopressin increases water permeability of the collecting duct. As tubular fluid passes through the hypertonic renal medulla, water leaves and the osmolality of the remaining fluid rises.

notes.A: The tip of a long loop of Henle lies in hypertonic medulla. Its fluid is ordinarily more concentrated than plasma during antidiuresis.
notes.B: Bowman’s space contains filtrate close to plasma osmolality. Fluid arriving at the early distal tubule is usually more dilute after salt reabsorption without water.
notes.D: The proximal tubule reabsorbs solute and water together. Its tubular fluid does not show a large progressive rise in osmolality.
notes.E: Proximal fluid is approximately iso-osmotic with plasma, even though individual solutes change concentration.

questions.stem: Transport maximum (Tmax) - limited reabsorption of a substance implies that its:

options.label: B
options.text: reabsorption is critically related to tubular transit time

options.label: D
options.text: renal clearance falls with its plasma concentration

options.label: E
options.text: reabsorption is carried out by the mechanism of facilitated diffusion

questions.why: A transport maximum exists for carrier-mediated active transport (e.g., glucose reabsorption).

notes.B: Tm is a carrier limit, not a time limit.
notes.C: Passive transport has no Tm.
notes.D: Clearance RISES above Tm.
notes.E: Tm implies an active carrier here.

questions.stem: The cells of the distal convoluted tubule:

options.label: A
options.text: reabsorb about 50% of the water filtered by the glomeruli

options.label: D
options.text: reabsorb sodium in exchange for hydrogen or potassium ions

options.label: E
options.text: determine the final composition of urine

questions.why: The distal tubule (and collecting duct) reabsorbs sodium in exchange for secreting potassium (under aldosterone) or hydrogen.

notes.A: The proximal tubule does that.
notes.B: Done proximally.
notes.C: Done proximally.
notes.E: The collecting duct finalises urine.

questions.stem: Urea:

options.label: A
options.text: and glucose have different molar concentrations in normal blood

options.label: B
options.text: clearance is higher, than creatinins one

options.label: C
options.text: is actively secreted by the renal tubular cells into the tubular fluid

options.label: D
options.text: concentration in blood may rise ten-fold after a high protein meal

options.label: E
options.text: causes diuresis when its blood concentration is increased

questions.why: Urea in the tubular lumen acts as an osmole. When an increase in plasma urea leads to a high filtered and excreted urea load, some water remains in the lumen and urine output can rise through osmotic diuresis.

notes.A: The normal molar ranges for urea and glucose overlap. Their measured concentrations depend on feeding, protein turnover and kidney handling.
notes.B: Urea is reabsorbed in parts of the nephron. Its clearance is usually below that of creatinine.
notes.C: Urea recycling is largely mediated by passive urea transporters. Movement into selected thin limbs is not generally described as active secretion.
notes.D: A high-protein meal can increase urea production, but a tenfold rise in blood urea is not the usual response.

questions.stem: In healthy people, urinary:

options.label: A
options.text: clearance of glucose differs 0, if its plasma concentration is below 11mmol·l-1

options.label: C
options.text: colour is due to small quantities of bile pigments

options.label: D
options.text: pH falls as dietary protein rises

options.label: E
options.text: calcium excretion is decreased by parathormone

questions.why: High protein diets increase acid production (from amino acid metabolism), which lowers urinary pH.

notes.A: Below threshold glucose clearance is zero.
notes.B: Range is about 50–1200.
notes.C: Colour is urochrome.
notes.E: PTH DECREASES calcium excretion.

questions.stem: Diabetes insipidus (deficiency of antidiuretic hormone) causes a fall in the:

options.label: B
options.text: reabsorption of water from the proximal tubules

options.label: C
options.text: extracellular but not intracellular fluid volume

questions.why: Central diabetes insipidus reduces vasopressin delivery to the collecting ducts. Less aquaporin-2 is inserted, so less water is reabsorbed and a large volume of dilute, low-osmolality urine is produced.

notes.B: Proximal water reabsorption largely follows solute. The principal variable vasopressin-sensitive step is farther downstream.
notes.C: Unreplaced free-water loss can raise extracellular osmolality and pull water out of cells. Both fluid compartments may contract.
notes.D: Extracellular fluid osmolality can rise if free-water loss is not matched by intake, sometimes producing hypernatraemia.
notes.E: Cells lose water when the surrounding fluid becomes hypertonic. Their solutes become more concentrated rather than diluted.

questions.stem: Drugs which interfere with active transport of sodium in the proximal tubule tend to increase:
questions.why: Interfering with proximal sodium reabsorption leaves more sodium and accompanying anions in the tubular lumen. This limits water reabsorption and tends to increase downstream delivery and urine flow, although distal segments can partly compensate.

notes.B: The effect on plasma osmolality depends on relative water and electrolyte losses and subsequent intake. Increased tubular flow is the more direct effect.
notes.C: Reduced sodium transport usually also reduces some proximal chloride reabsorption. It does not directly increase chloride recovery there.
notes.D: If sodium and water losses persist, extracellular fluid volume tends to fall, including the interstitial compartment.
notes.E: Plasma volume generally falls if a loss of extracellular sodium and water is sustained.

questions.stem: Reabsorption of amino acids from the filtrate requires many different protein carriers because:

options.label: C
options.text: there are only 10 different amino acids

options.label: D
options.text: transport of amino acids is typically highly specific

questions.why: Proximal tubular cells use several amino acid transport systems with different affinities for neutral, acidic, basic and other groups of amino acids. Substrates with similar structures may share and compete for the same carrier.

notes.A: Amino acids are individual solutes, not folded proteins that need transporters to avoid denaturation.
notes.B: Amino acids can compete for shared transporters. Competition and selectivity help explain why several systems are used.
notes.C: There are twenty standard protein-forming amino acids, and specialised transporter systems handle groups with similar properties.
notes.E: Glucose has separate sodium-linked transporters. This does not explain the variety of amino acid carriers.

questions.stem: Reabsorption (transport) of both Na+ and glucose together from the renal lumen is an example of:
questions.why: Sodium and glucose enter the proximal tubular cell from the lumen in the same direction through SGLT proteins. The basolateral sodium pump creates the sodium gradient that powers this secondary active symport.

notes.A: Facilitated diffusion moves a solute down its gradient without energetic coupling. SGLT can move glucose uphill by coupling it to sodium entry.
notes.B: The sodium gradient provides usable energy for uphill glucose uptake. This is conventionally classified as secondary active transport.
notes.C: The apical cotransporter uses the sodium gradient without hydrolysing ATP. Direct ATP use occurs at the basolateral sodium pump.
notes.D: Antiport moves the coupled solutes in opposite directions. Sodium and glucose move together from lumen into cell.

questions.stem: All statements about ADH are correct, except:

options.label: A
options.text: is secreted by the posterior pituitary

options.label: B
options.text: its secretion is regulated by plasma osmolality

options.label: C
options.text: increases the tubular reabsorption of K+

options.label: D
options.text: increases reabsorption of water in the distal and collecting tubules

questions.why: The characteristic renal action of vasopressin is to increase water reabsorption in the late distal nephron and collecting ducts through V2 receptors and aquaporin-2. Increased tubular potassium reabsorption is not its defining action.

notes.A: The posterior pituitary releases vasopressin into blood after the hormone travels there from hypothalamic neurons.
notes.B: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors respond to plasma tonicity. Reduced effective circulating volume can also stimulate vasopressin release.
notes.D: Vasopressin increases apical aquaporin-2 in principal cells, raising water permeability in the late distal nephron and collecting system.
notes.E: Vasopressin is synthesised in hypothalamic nuclei and then carried along axons to the posterior pituitary.

questions.stem: The transport maximum of glucose (TmaxGl) is:
questions.why: The glucose transport maximum is the maximum rate at which both kidneys can reabsorb filtered glucose once transporters are saturated. The usual teaching estimate is about 300–375 milligrams per minute, with variation among individuals.

notes.A: A value of about 125 millilitres per minute describes GFR. A glucose transport maximum is measured as mass per time.
notes.C: Millimoles per litre are units of glucose concentration. The transport maximum represents mass of glucose reabsorbed per time.
notes.D: A plasma concentration of this order is closer to a threshold for glucosuria. The transport maximum describes the total mass reabsorbed per minute.
notes.E: The range expressed in milligrams per minute has the correct units and is near the conventional maximum reabsorptive rate.

questions.stem: The human kidneys can concentrate the final urine up to:
questions.why: Under strong vasopressin stimulation, human kidneys can produce urine near 1,200 milliosmoles per kilogram of water. Collecting-duct water reabsorption and the medullary osmotic gradient allow the final urine to concentrate. The option uses the approximate litre-based equivalent.

notes.A: An osmolality near 100 milliosmoles per kilogram describes dilute urine with little vasopressin effect.
notes.B: A value near 120 milliosmoles per kilogram is also below plasma osmolality and represents dilute rather than concentrated urine.
notes.C: About 295 milliosmoles per kilogram is close to plasma osmolality. Concentrated urine can reach several times this value.
notes.D: The numerical range near 7.4 is familiar as blood pH. It is not a measurement of urine concentration.

questions.stem: What is the percentage of water reabsorbed in the tubules, under the control of ADH?
questions.why: Vasopressin regulates the facultative portion of water reabsorption in the late distal nephron and collecting ducts. A value around 15 percent of the original filtered water is a rough teaching estimate of the adjustable fraction. The amount actually reabsorbed varies with vasopressin and solute handling.

notes.A: Much of the filtered water is recovered before the vasopressin-sensitive segments, so the hormone does not directly govern all reabsorption.
notes.B: A large proportion of water follows solute in relatively fixed-permeability segments. That portion is largely independent of vasopressin.
notes.C: More than half the filtered water is already reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. The facultative fraction farther downstream is substantially smaller.
notes.E: Vasopressin can make a substantial difference to collecting-duct water uptake. The adjustable fraction is therefore not zero.

questions.stem: Glucose and amino acids are reabsorbed in the:
questions.why: The proximal tubule reabsorbs almost all filtered glucose and amino acids under normal conditions. It uses glucose-specific and amino-acid-specific transport systems, many driven by the inward sodium gradient.

notes.B: The distal tubule principally adjusts electrolyte handling. Most filtered glucose and amino acids have already been reclaimed upstream.
notes.C: Collecting tubules adjust water, sodium, potassium and acid–base balance. They are not the main site of nutrient recovery.
notes.D: The loop of Henle helps build the medullary gradient through its segmental salt and water transport.
notes.E: Filtered glucose is normally recovered efficiently by proximal sodium–glucose cotransporters.

questions.stem: The human kidneys can dilute the final urine up to:
questions.why: When vasopressin is low, the collecting duct remains relatively impermeable to water. Sodium chloride is removed upstream without water, so urine can be diluted to roughly 50–100 milliosmoles per kilogram of water. The listed value near 100 represents dilute urine.

notes.A: Millilitres per minute are units of fluid flow. Dilution is assessed by measuring the concentration of solutes in urine.
notes.C: Around 295 milliosmoles per kilogram is close to plasma osmolality and is substantially above the attainable dilute urine range.
notes.D: The values 7.36–7.44 are expressed as pH. They do not describe urine osmolality.
notes.E: About 1,200 milliosmoles per kilogram is near maximal concentration of human urine, reached in strong antidiuresis.

questions.stem: Which of the following are reabsorbed in the ascending limb of the loop of Henle:
questions.why: In the thick ascending limb, NKCC2 transports sodium, potassium and chloride from the lumen into epithelial cells. Some potassium recycles into the lumen, but the segment reabsorbs these solutes overall with very little accompanying water.

notes.A: Sodium is reabsorbed through apical NKCC2, driven indirectly by the basolateral sodium–potassium ATPase.
notes.B: Potassium enters cells via NKCC2. Some is returned to the lumen through ROMK, helping sustain cotransport and the lumen-positive voltage.
notes.C: Chloride enters through NKCC2 and leaves across the basolateral membrane, contributing to net salt removal from the lumen.
notes.D: The ascending limb is relatively impermeable to water. Removing salt without water dilutes the tubular fluid.

questions.stem: Which of the following is/are reabsorbed in the descending limb of the loop of Henle:
questions.why: The water-permeable thin descending limb allows water to move into the hypertonic medullary interstitium. This concentrates the descending tubular fluid. The major active recovery of sodium chloride occurs in the thick ascending limb instead.

notes.A: The thin descending limb is not the principal active sodium-reabsorbing segment. Net sodium chloride removal is characteristic of the ascending limb.
notes.B: Active chloride recovery via NKCC2 occurs in the thick ascending limb. Water removal characterises the usual descending-limb model.
notes.C: Most loop calcium reabsorption occurs paracellularly in the thick ascending limb, driven by the lumen-positive voltage.
notes.D: Potassium is handled prominently in the proximal tubule and thick ascending limb. Water movement is the distinctive descending-limb function.

questions.stem: Which statement is correct:

options.label: A
options.text: the loop of Henle is permeable for salts and weakly permeable for water

options.label: B
options.text: the descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable for Na+ and K+ and weakly permeable for CL-

options.label: C
options.text: the thick segment of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable for ions

options.label: D
options.text: the ascending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable for water and weakly permeable for ions

options.label: E
options.text: the descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable for salts and weakly permeable for water

questions.why: The thick ascending limb transports sodium, potassium and chloride through NKCC2 and is relatively impermeable to water. Net ion removal without water dilutes the filtrate and helps establish a concentrated medullary interstitium.

notes.A: The loop has different properties in its descending and ascending limbs. The entire loop does not share a single low water permeability.
notes.B: The classic distinction is that the thin descending limb is more permeable to water, whereas active salt transport is prominent in the ascending limb.
notes.D: The ascending limb is relatively impermeable to water and removes salt from the lumen.
notes.E: Water permeability is a defining property of much of the thin descending limb. Its handling of salts differs from active transport by the thick ascending limb.

questions.stem: The concentration of the final urine is due to:

options.label: A
options.text: the countercurrent multiplying mechanism in the loop of Henle

options.label: B
options.text: the countercurrent exchanger of vasa recta

questions.why: The loop of Henle multiplies the medullary osmotic gradient, the vasa recta limit washout by countercurrent exchange, and vasopressin increases collecting-duct water permeability. Together these mechanisms permit concentrated final urine. Medullary urea recycling also helps maintain the gradient.

notes.A: Salt reabsorption without water in the thick ascending limb helps build the medullary gradient used to concentrate urine.
notes.B: The vasa recta exchange water and solutes as blood passes through the medulla. This helps preserve the established gradient.
notes.C: Vasopressin increases collecting-duct aquaporin-2. Water then moves down its osmotic gradient into the interstitium.
notes.D: Hydrostatic and oncotic pressures affect peritubular capillary uptake. They do not substitute for the medullary gradient and regulated duct permeability.

questions.stem: Renin is secreted by:

options.label: E
options.text: cells in the peritubular capillary bed

questions.why: Renin is secreted by juxtaglomerular granular cells, specialised vascular smooth muscle cells located mainly in the afferent arteriole near the glomerulus. Reduced perfusion, beta-1 stimulation and low macula densa salt delivery can drive release.

notes.A: Macula densa cells sense distal tubular sodium chloride and signal to adjacent granular cells. The granular cells are the usual renin source.
notes.B: The proximal tubule performs bulk reabsorption and contributes to local renin–angiotensin pathways. Circulating renin chiefly comes from granular cells.
notes.C: Distal tubular cells help regulate electrolyte delivery. The specialised renin-secreting cells are in the neighbouring arteriolar wall.
notes.E: Peritubular capillaries collect reabsorbed fluid. Renin is released from granular cells primarily on the afferent arteriolar side.

questions.stem: Renin release:

options.label: A
options.text: is promoted by reduced arteriolar stretch in the glomeruli

options.label: B
options.text: increases when systemic arterial pressure rises

options.label: D
options.text: tends to expand the plasma volume

questions.why: Reduced stretch of the afferent arteriolar wall stimulates granular cells to release renin. The resulting angiotensin II and aldosterone responses promote sodium and water retention, which can expand or restore plasma volume.

notes.A: Juxtaglomerular cells sense reduced stretch in the afferent arteriole near the glomerulus and increase renin release.
notes.B: Increased renal perfusion tends to suppress renin release through the arteriolar pressure-sensing mechanism.
notes.C: Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to form angiotensin I. Angiotensin-converting enzyme then acts on angiotensin I independently.
notes.D: Angiotensin II and aldosterone increase renal sodium retention, and water follows. This helps restore effective circulating volume.

questions.stem: Aldosterone:

options.label: A
options.text: is a steroid hormone secreted by the adrenal medulla

options.label: B
options.text: production ceases following removal of the kidneys and their juxtaglomerular cells

options.label: C
options.text: production increases during treatment with ACE inhibitors

options.label: D
options.text: secretion results in increased potassium reabsorption by the nephron

options.label: E
options.text: secretion results in increased plasma volume

questions.why: Aldosterone acts in the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron to increase sodium reabsorption and promote potassium secretion. Sodium retention tends to expand extracellular and plasma volume, although compensatory mechanisms limit sustained retention.

notes.A: Aldosterone is a steroid of the adrenal cortex, produced in the zona glomerulosa. The adrenal medulla produces catecholamines.
notes.B: Renal renin is a major stimulus through angiotensin II, but extracellular potassium can directly stimulate aldosterone production in the adrenal cortex.
notes.C: ACE inhibition lowers angiotensin II and usually reduces its stimulus to aldosterone secretion, especially early after starting treatment.
notes.D: Aldosterone generally increases distal potassium secretion into urine when sodium delivery and other conditions permit.

questions.stem: Secretion of renin:

options.label: A
options.text: occurs in the stomach during infancy

options.label: B
options.text: is stimulated by the hormone angiotensin I

options.label: C
options.text: is stimulated by a fall in extracellular fluid volume and leads to raised levels of angiotensin II in the blood

options.label: E
options.text: inhibits ACTH secretion by the pituitary gland

questions.why: Reduced extracellular volume can decrease renal perfusion and increase sympathetic drive. Juxtaglomerular cells respond by releasing renin, which increases formation of angiotensin I and consequently angiotensin II.

notes.A: Renin is a renal protease in the angiotensin pathway. The historical milk-coagulating enzyme rennin is chymosin and is a different enzyme.
notes.B: Angiotensin I is a product of renin activity. Angiotensin II generally provides negative feedback on renin release.
notes.D: Renin supports formation of angiotensin II, which stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex.
notes.E: The main effect of renin is activation of the angiotensin pathway. Pituitary ACTH release is regulated primarily by hypothalamic and glucocorticoid feedback.

questions.stem: All statements about aldosterone are correct except:

options.label: A
options.text: is secreted by the adrenal cortex

options.label: B
options.text: acts on distal and collective tubules

options.label: D
options.text: increases the tubular reabsorption of K+

options.label: E
options.text: its secretion is controlled by angiotensin II

questions.why: Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption in the late distal nephron and collecting ducts. The resulting electrical gradient, together with direct effects on transport proteins, generally increases potassium secretion rather than potassium recovery.

notes.A: Aldosterone is secreted by the adrenal cortex, specifically by its outer zona glomerulosa.
notes.B: The aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron comprises late distal segments and the collecting system.
notes.C: Aldosterone increases epithelial sodium channel activity and basolateral sodium pump activity in principal cells, promoting sodium reabsorption.
notes.E: Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone production when effective volume is low. Elevated plasma potassium also stimulates it directly.

questions.stem: The secretion of renin is stimulated by:

options.label: E
options.text: increased Na+ in the tubular fluid

questions.why: Increased renal sympathetic activity activates beta-1 receptors on juxtaglomerular granular cells and promotes renin release. This supports the renin–angiotensin response during states such as decreased effective circulating volume.

notes.A: Sympathetic beta-1 stimulation is the relevant direct neural trigger. Increased parasympathetic tone is not the usual renin signal.
notes.C: Expansion of extracellular volume usually suppresses renin by increasing perfusion and reducing the need for sodium retention.
notes.D: Decreased adrenaline does not provide the usual beta-adrenergic stimulus. Renal sympathetic nerves mainly release noradrenaline locally.
notes.E: Increased sodium chloride delivery to the macula densa generally suppresses renin. Reduced delivery stimulates it.

questions.stem: The atrial natriuretic peptide has/have the following effect/effects:

options.label: A
options.text: increase the reabsorption of Na+ and water

options.label: B
options.text: increase the excretion of Na+ and water

questions.why: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released with atrial stretch. It promotes urinary sodium and water excretion by altering renal haemodynamics and tubular sodium handling and by restraining renin and aldosterone. It can also relax vascular smooth muscle.

notes.A: The principal renal response is natriuresis, with water following the excreted sodium. Increased reabsorption is the opposite effect.
notes.B: Atrial natriuretic peptide increases sodium excretion and can increase water output, helping relieve atrial stretch.
notes.C: Atrial natriuretic peptide can relax systemic vascular smooth muscle through cyclic GMP. Individual renal vascular segments can respond differently.
notes.E: This group includes increased sodium and water reabsorption, which conflicts with the principal natriuretic action.

questions.stem: In the juxtaglomerular apparatus are found:
questions.why: Juxtaglomerular cells have beta-1 adrenergic receptors that stimulate renin release.

notes.A: Not the main renin receptor.
notes.B: Not the main renin receptor.
notes.D: Not the main renin receptor.
notes.E: Not present on JG cells.

questions.stem: Renin is secreted by:
questions.why: The juxtaglomerular apparatus contains specialised granular cells, mostly in the wall of the afferent arteriole. These cells secrete renin in response to low perfusion or other signals for activation of the renin–angiotensin system.

notes.A: Juxtaglomerular describes the location of the granular cells and associated apparatus. The standard nephron classes are cortical and juxtamedullary.
notes.B: The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines. Renin originates chiefly from specialised renal arteriolar cells.
notes.D: The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone in response to angiotensin II. It is downstream of renal renin release.
notes.E: The hypothalamus produces vasopressin and neuroendocrine signals, while circulating renin is released chiefly by the kidney.

questions.stem: Which of the following causes hyperkalemia?
questions.why: Working skeletal muscle releases potassium during repeated action potentials. Vigorous exercise can therefore raise plasma potassium transiently, with uptake by muscle and other cells helping normalise it during recovery.

notes.B: Alkalaemia often promotes movement of potassium into cells, tending to lower plasma potassium.
notes.C: Insulin stimulates cellular potassium uptake, partly through the sodium–potassium ATPase, and tends to lower plasma potassium.
notes.D: Hypertonicity can cause water to leave cells and can favour potassium movement outward. A decrease in osmolality does not typically cause that shift.
notes.E: Beta-2 agonists promote cellular potassium uptake and usually decrease the measured plasma potassium concentration.

questions.stem: Dialysis fluid used in the treatment of renal failure should contain the normal plasma levels of:
questions.why: Dialysis fluid is isotonic to plasma to prevent net fluid shifts (osmotic damage to blood cells).

notes.A: Urea should be ABSENT to remove it.
notes.B: K+ is set low.
notes.D: Proteins are not included.
notes.E: Buffer (bicarbonate) is added to remove acid.

questions.stem: Drinking a litre of water:

options.label: E
options.text: decreases the specific gravity of the body

questions.why: Once absorbed, a litre of plain water transiently increases body water relative to sodium and lowers plasma sodium concentration and tonicity. Vasopressin release falls and the kidneys excrete the excess as dilute urine.

notes.A: A fall in plasma tonicity suppresses vasopressin release. Collecting ducts then become less permeable to water.
notes.C: Water loading normally promotes dilute urine, so urine osmolality decreases instead of increasing.
notes.D: If extracellular tonicity falls, water moves into cells and they can swell slightly. They do not shrink from this stimulus.
notes.E: Whole-body specific gravity is not a direct or predictable measure of a water load. The immediate measurable effect is dilution of extracellular solutes.

questions.stem: A rise in the osmolality of extracellular fluid may lead to:

options.label: B
options.text: increased water reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubules

options.label: D
options.text: an increase in intracellular fluid volume

questions.why: Hyperosmolality is detected by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, triggering thirst and ADH (vasopressin) release.

notes.B: Proximal water reabsorption is not ADH-dependent.
notes.C: Vasopressin RISES.
notes.D: ICF SHRINKS.
notes.E: Not a response to raised osmolality.

questions.stem: Sodium retention:

options.label: A
options.text: occurs for several days after major surgery

questions.why: Sodium retention increases extracellular sodium content and is usually accompanied by water retention. This can expand both interstitial fluid and blood volume and aggravate oedema. Major surgery can produce a temporary sodium-retaining stress response.

notes.A: After major surgery, stress responses and changes in effective circulating volume can promote transient renal sodium retention.
notes.B: Retained sodium is largely extracellular. Associated water retention expands the extracellular compartment.
notes.C: Plasma is part of the extracellular fluid and can expand when sodium and water are retained.
notes.D: Expansion of interstitial fluid can worsen oedema, especially when capillary or lymphatic function is impaired.

questions.stem: Sodium depletion differs from water depletion in that:

options.label: B
options.text: intracellular fluid volume is less affected

questions.why: Loss of relatively isotonic sodium-containing fluid primarily contracts extracellular volume and has less immediate effect on intracellular volume. Pure water loss raises extracellular tonicity, drawing water out of cells and shrinking the intracellular compartment.

notes.A: Sodium and extracellular volume depletion can produce prominent cardiovascular effects because they reduce effective circulating volume.
notes.C: Haemoconcentration can occur in both states, depending on the relative amount and site of fluid loss. It does not distinguish them reliably.
notes.D: Pure water depletion typically stimulates marked osmotic thirst. Sodium depletion may also stimulate thirst if effective circulating volume falls.
notes.E: Vasopressin responds to both tonicity and volume. Its level cannot be ranked without knowing the severity and type of losses.

questions.stem: A high blood potassium level (hyperkalaemia):

options.label: B
options.text: follows severe crush injuries to the limbs

options.label: C
options.text: may diminish cardiac performance and cause death

options.label: D
options.text: may be reduced by intravenous infusion of insulin and glucose

questions.why: Hyperkalaemia can result from reduced renal excretion or from potassium release by injured muscle. Severe elevations impair cardiac electrical conduction and can be fatal. Insulin can temporarily shift potassium into cells, with glucose used to reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia.

notes.A: Acute kidney failure can decrease potassium excretion and allow extracellular potassium to accumulate.
notes.B: Severe crush injury can release potassium from damaged muscle cells. Associated kidney injury can further limit clearance.
notes.C: High extracellular potassium can disrupt cardiac depolarisation and conduction, causing dangerous arrhythmias and sometimes cardiac arrest.
notes.D: Insulin increases cellular uptake of potassium. Glucose is given with it in typical treatment to reduce hypoglycaemia risk.

questions.stem: A raised level of calcium in the blood (hypercalcaemia):

options.label: A
options.text: may occur when parathyroid activity decreases

options.label: B
options.text: may occur when the plasma protein level falls

options.label: C
options.text: may occur in chronic renal failure

options.label: D
options.text: increases the risk of stone formation in the urinary tract

options.label: E
options.text: causes increased excitability of nerve and muscle

questions.why: Hypercalcemia increases urinary calcium excretion, predisposing to kidney stones.

notes.A: Low PTH causes LOW calcium.
notes.B: Low protein lowers TOTAL calcium.
notes.C: CRF usually causes LOW calcium.
notes.E: Excitability DECREASES.

questions.stem: Thirst is stimulated by:

options.label: A
options.text: increase in plasma osmolality and volume

options.label: B
options.text: increase in plasma osmolality and decrease in volume

options.label: C
options.text: decrease in osmolality and increase in volume

options.label: D
options.text: decrease in plasma osmolality and volume

questions.why: Rising plasma osmolality activates central osmoreceptors and drives thirst. A fall in effective circulating volume can also stimulate thirst through pressure and volume signals and increased angiotensin II. These are the two standard directions of change that promote drinking.

notes.A: Higher osmolality stimulates drinking. Expansion of effective volume usually opposes the volume-related thirst signal.
notes.C: Lower osmolality and higher effective circulating volume both generally suppress thirst.
notes.D: Reduced volume can stimulate thirst, but falling osmolality normally restrains it. These changes therefore have opposing effects.
notes.E: Osmotic thirst usually follows cellular dehydration due to extracellular hypertonicity, rather than an increase in cell volume.

questions.stem: The reference interval of plasma osmolarity is:
questions.why: Normal plasma osmolality is tightly regulated between 280 and 295 mOsm/kg.

notes.A: Too low.
notes.B: That is the GFR.
notes.D: That is a pH range.
notes.E: That is maximal urine osmolality.

questions.stem: When the intake of water and salts is normal:

options.label: A
options.text: the osmotic pressure of ECF is higher than that of ICF

options.label: B
options.text: the osmotic pressure ICF is higher than that of ECF

options.label: C
options.text: the osmotic pressure of ECF is equal to that of ICF

options.label: D
options.text: the volume of ECF is bigger than that of ICF

questions.why: Water moves freely across most cell membranes, so intracellular and extracellular fluids reach essentially the same effective osmotic pressure at steady state. Their solute compositions differ, and the intracellular compartment contains more of total body water.

notes.A: If extracellular fluid becomes hypertonic, water moves out of cells and tends to eliminate the effective osmotic gradient.
notes.B: If intracellular fluid becomes more concentrated than the surrounding fluid, water enters cells until the effective gradient is largely balanced.
notes.D: About two thirds of total body water is normally intracellular. The extracellular compartment is smaller.
notes.E: Near equality of effective osmotic pressures is the expected steady state when fluid intake and losses are balanced.
