questions.stem: All but except one are followed by thirst:
questions.why: Hypervolemia (increased blood volume) suppresses thirst, whereas the other factors stimulate it.

notes.A: A strong thirst trigger.
notes.B: A strong thirst trigger.
notes.C: Released alongside thirst.
notes.E: Causes thirst.

questions.stem: The volume of ECF is regulated by:
questions.why: Extracellular fluid volume is regulated mainly through renal sodium balance and its accompanying water. The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and sympathetic responses favour retention when effective volume is low, while atrial natriuretic peptide promotes sodium loss during expansion.

notes.A: Renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone increase sodium retention when effective circulating volume falls.
notes.B: Atrial stretch promotes release of atrial natriuretic peptide, which increases renal sodium excretion and opposes volume expansion.
notes.C: Catecholamines can influence renal vascular tone and stimulate renin under adrenergic control, contributing to volume regulation.
notes.D: Renal sympathetic nerves influence renin release, tubular sodium reabsorption and renal haemodynamics.

questions.stem: The information about the extracellular volume and its Na+ content is processed in the:
questions.why: The posterior hypothalamus is involved in regulating ECF volume and thirst.

notes.A: The lateral hypothalamus is linked to thirst and feeding.
notes.B: The anterior hypothalamus holds the osmoreceptors.
notes.D: The thalamus is a relay.
notes.E: The hippocampus is for memory.

questions.stem: The acid-buffering power:

options.label: A
options.text: of HCO3- in blood is increased by respiratory control of pCO2

options.label: B
options.text: of haemoglobin exceeds that of HCO3- in blood

options.label: C
options.text: of HCO3- is increased by the action of carbonic anhydrase

options.label: D
options.text: of venous blood is normally greater than that of arterial blood

questions.why: The bicarbonate buffer system is highly effective due to respiratory control of CO2. Hemoglobin is also a major buffer, especially in venous blood.

notes.A: True, but B and D are also true.
notes.B: True, but A and D are also true.
notes.C: The enzyme speeds the reaction but does not add buffering power.
notes.D: True, but A and B are also true.

questions.stem: A drug which inhibits carbonic anhydrase:

options.label: A
options.text: decreases bicarbonate formation and reabsorption in the kidney

options.label: D
options.text: decreases urinary loss of potassium ions

questions.why: Renal carbonic anhydrase helps proximal tubular cells reclaim filtered bicarbonate by accelerating interconversion of carbon dioxide and bicarbonate. Inhibition decreases bicarbonate reabsorption, so more bicarbonate is excreted and plasma bicarbonate can fall.

notes.B: Urinary bicarbonate loss can decrease plasma bicarbonate rather than increasing it.
notes.C: Loss of bicarbonate tends to lower systemic pH and can produce hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis.
notes.D: Greater distal sodium delivery can increase potassium secretion and loss. Potassium conservation is not the usual effect.
notes.E: Bicarbonate remaining in the lumen can increase urine pH and promote diuresis, especially early after inhibition.

questions.stem: A long-standing increase in arterial pCO2 (respiratory acidosis) leads to:

options.label: A
options.text: an increase in renal bicarbonate formation

options.label: B
options.text: a decrease in urinary ammonium salts

options.label: C
options.text: a decrease in plasma potassium concentration

options.label: D
options.text: an increase of the monohydrogen/dihydrogen phosphate ratio in urine

options.label: E
options.text: an increase in urinary bicarbonate excretion

questions.why: With sustained respiratory acidosis, the kidneys compensate by increasing net acid excretion and adding newly generated bicarbonate to the blood. Increased ammonium excretion is a major part of this adaptation.

notes.B: Ammonium excretion normally increases as part of renal compensation for a persistent acid load.
notes.C: A fall in plasma potassium is not the defining renal compensation. Potassium changes depend on several additional factors.
notes.D: Excreted hydrogen ions shift urinary phosphate toward the protonated form, dihydrogen phosphate. This decreases the monohydrogen-to-dihydrogen ratio.
notes.E: Renal compensation conserves and generates bicarbonate. Increasing its urinary excretion would oppose correction of the acidaemia.

questions.stem: An acid-base buffer system:

options.label: A
options.text: can be a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base

options.label: B
options.text: can be a solution of sodium and chloride ions

options.label: C
options.text: prevents any change in pH when acid is added

options.label: D
options.text: works best when the pH is far from its pKa

questions.why: A weak acid and its conjugate base form a buffer because the base can accept added hydrogen ions and the acid can donate hydrogen ions when base is added. Buffering is usually greatest when the pH is near the pKa.

notes.B: Sodium chloride dissociates into ions that supply little buffering near physiological pH. It does not provide a suitable weak acid–base pair.
notes.C: A buffer limits pH changes rather than preventing them entirely. Its capacity is finite.
notes.D: A buffer works best near its pKa, when appreciable amounts of both the acid and the conjugate base are present.
notes.E: Intracellular proteins and phosphate can act as buffers within cells.

questions.stem: Acidosis in a patient may lead to:

options.label: C
options.text: a blood pH of less than 5.5

options.label: D
options.text: an urinary pH of less than 5.5

questions.why: In acidosis, the kidneys excrete excess H+ into the urine, resulting in an acidic urinary pH (often below 5.5).

notes.A: Acidosis REDUCES K+ excretion acutely.
notes.B: Acidosis causes HYPERventilation.
notes.C: Incompatible with life.
notes.E: Tetany goes with ALKALOSIS.

questions.stem: A raised blood pH and bicarbonate level is consistent with:

options.label: D
options.text: chronic renal failure with a raised pCO2

options.label: E
options.text: a history of persistent vomiting of gastric contents

questions.why: Persistent vomiting can remove hydrochloric acid from the stomach, producing metabolic alkalosis with raised bicarbonate and pH. Associated chloride and volume depletion can maintain the alkalosis by limiting renal bicarbonate excretion.

notes.A: Primary metabolic acidosis involves a fall in plasma bicarbonate and generally lowers blood pH.
notes.B: In respiratory alkalosis, a primary decrease in carbon dioxide raises pH. Renal compensation lowers bicarbonate.
notes.C: Lower carbon dioxide alone produces respiratory alkalosis. It does not account for an elevated bicarbonate in a simple disorder.
notes.D: Kidney failure commonly promotes metabolic acidosis. A raised carbon dioxide concentration also favours acidaemia rather than explaining alkalosis.

questions.stem: A patient with partly compensated respiratory acidosis:

options.label: B
options.text: must have a raised bicarbonate concentration [HCO3-]

options.label: C
options.text: may have evidence of renal compensation.

options.label: D
options.text: may have respiratory failure due to hypoventilation

questions.why: In simple partly compensated respiratory acidosis, carbon dioxide is elevated and blood pH is still low. Bicarbonate rises through immediate buffering and, if the disturbance persists, increased renal net acid excretion and bicarbonate retention.

notes.A: Raised arterial carbon dioxide is the primary disturbance in respiratory acidosis.
notes.B: Higher bicarbonate is the expected compensatory direction in simple respiratory acidosis. A separate metabolic disorder can alter that pattern.
notes.C: A persistent rise in carbon dioxide can stimulate renal bicarbonate generation and retention, so evidence of renal compensation may be present.
notes.D: Alveolar hypoventilation can raise arterial carbon dioxide and may occur with respiratory failure.

questions.stem: The acid-base balance is maintained by:
questions.why: Chemical buffers act rapidly to limit changes in pH. Ventilation regulates carbon dioxide, while renal bicarbonate handling and net acid excretion provide longer-term regulation. All three contribute to acid–base balance.

notes.A: Bicarbonate, proteins and phosphate are buffers in body fluids. They limit rapid changes in hydrogen ion concentration.
notes.B: Ventilation regulates arterial carbon dioxide, which is the respiratory component of bicarbonate buffering.
notes.C: The kidneys reclaim filtered bicarbonate, generate new bicarbonate and excrete net acid.
notes.D: Buffering and renal regulation are both important. This combination leaves out respiratory control of carbon dioxide.

questions.stem: For the buffer capacity of the blood of highest significance is the:
questions.why: The bicarbonate–carbon dioxide system is the principal extracellular physiological buffer because ventilation controls carbon dioxide and the kidneys regulate bicarbonate. Haemoglobin provides substantial non-bicarbonate buffering within red cells.

notes.A: Haemoglobin buffers hydrogen ions in erythrocytes and assists carbon dioxide transport. It is a major non-bicarbonate buffer.
notes.B: Plasma and cellular proteins contribute to buffering through ionisable groups, but whole-body control of extracellular pH centres on bicarbonate and carbon dioxide.
notes.C: Phosphate buffers intracellular fluid and contributes to titratable acid in urine. Its plasma concentration is relatively low.
notes.E: The ammonium system is important for renal net acid excretion. It is not the main extracellular blood buffer.

questions.stem: The H+ ions are excreted in the tubular fluid as a result of:
questions.why: Tubular epithelial cells secrete hydrogen ions into the lumen using apical exchangers and proton pumps. Much of the net acid excreted is buffered as ammonium or titratable acid rather than remaining as free hydrogen ions.

notes.A: Filtration carries only a very small free hydrogen-ion load at plasma pH. Most urinary acid is added by tubular processes.
notes.B: Reabsorption is movement out of the lumen toward blood. It does not explain addition of hydrogen ions to tubular fluid.
notes.D: Secretion adds hydrogen ions to the lumen, whereas reabsorption is in the opposite direction.
notes.E: Tubular hydrogen-ion secretion is a recognised part of renal acid–base regulation and contributes to net acid excretion.

questions.stem: HCO3- are excreted in the tubular fluid as a result of:
questions.why: Bicarbonate is freely filtered at the glomerulus. (Most is then reabsorbed).

notes.B: Reabsorption REMOVES it from the tubular fluid.
notes.C: HCO3- is not secreted in the proximal tubule.
notes.D: Only filtration.
notes.E: Option A is correct.

questions.stem: The secretion of H+ in the tubular fluid is achieved by:
questions.why: Renal hydrogen-ion secretion uses both primary and secondary active transport. Apical proton ATPases directly use ATP, while the sodium–hydrogen exchanger uses the inward sodium gradient ultimately maintained by the sodium–potassium ATPase.

notes.A: Hydrogen-ion secretion depends on specific transport proteins. Osmosis describes water movement and cannot account for this ion flux.
notes.B: Primary active proton pumps contribute, but diffusion is not the other major pathway. Sodium–hydrogen exchange is a secondary active mechanism.
notes.D: Secondary active exchange contributes to proximal secretion, but distal proton ATPases also provide primary active secretion.
notes.E: Secondary active transport is one contributor. Osmosis and simple diffusion do not replace the direct proton pumps.

questions.stem: In acidosis, the kidneys:

options.label: A
options.text: increase the excretion of H+ and HCO3-

options.label: B
options.text: decrease the excretion of H+ and increase the reabsorption of HCO3-

options.label: C
options.text: increase the excretion of H+ and reabsorption of HCO3-

options.label: D
options.text: decrease the excretion of H+ and reabsorption of HCO3-

questions.why: With intact renal function, acidosis increases tubular hydrogen-ion secretion and conservation of filtered bicarbonate. Increased ammonium and titratable acid excretion remove acid and add newly generated bicarbonate to the blood.

notes.A: Increased net acid excretion is appropriate, but losing more bicarbonate would worsen the disturbance.
notes.B: Bicarbonate recovery is appropriate, but a decrease in net hydrogen-ion excretion would limit compensation.
notes.D: Decreasing both acid excretion and bicarbonate recovery would oppose the usual renal correction of acidosis.
notes.E: The normal response combines increased acid elimination with enhanced bicarbonate conservation and generation.

questions.stem: In alcalosis, the kidneys:

options.label: A
options.text: decrease the excretion of H+ and increase the reabsorption of HCO3-

options.label: C
options.text: increase the excretion of H+ and decrease the excretion of HCO3-

options.label: D
options.text: increase the indirect reabsorption of HCO3-

options.label: E
options.text: decrease the excretion of H+ and increase the excretion of HCO3-

questions.why: When renal function and effective volume are adequate, alkalosis decreases net acid excretion and favours excretion of bicarbonate. Type B intercalated cells can secrete bicarbonate. Chloride or volume depletion can limit this response and sustain an alkalosis.

notes.A: Decreasing acid excretion helps correct alkalosis, but increasing bicarbonate reabsorption would retain excess base.
notes.B: An increase in net acid excretion would increase body bicarbonate and tend to perpetuate alkalosis.
notes.C: Greater acid excretion with lower bicarbonate excretion increases body bicarbonate and worsens the disturbance.
notes.D: Increased bicarbonate reabsorption would retain base. Correction generally requires greater bicarbonate excretion when the conditions for it are present.
